overview: The Romanian state grew from the 1859 union of Wallachia and Moldavia and later passed through monarchy, dictatorship and republican government. This map record begins in 1878. Schools, postal buildings, family crafts and surviving documents reveal how institutions and everyday life changed across its long modern history.

periods.title: Monarchy and changing society
periods.summary: Royal institutions, schools and communications developed, while war and dictatorship brought persecution and catastrophe.

periods.title: Communist government
periods.summary: The monarchy ended with forced abdication in 1947; the royal palace was nationalized and later used as a museum.

periods.title: A continuing republic
periods.summary: The upheaval of 1989 was followed by the 1991 Constitution and continuing republican institutions.

sections.title: Schoolwork and the objects around it

items.text: Casa Școalelor was established in 1896 to support primary-school construction and manage education funds. Money came from state support and donations. Expanding education required buildings and reliable funding, not simply announcing that children should learn.

A school-prize medal dated 1927 to 1930 shows an open book, inkwell and writing quill. Its Romanian inscription PREMIUL I means “First prize.” This small object preserves both a written-language sample and the public celebration of a pupil’s achievement.

Designs dated 1947 in the museum’s collection show pupils in a classroom and girls at a loom. They were prepared for educational fundraising stamps. These are images of the education promoted by their makers, not photographs of every Romanian classroom.

Romania’s first postage-due stamps appeared in 1881 in six denominations. Postal staff used this kind of stamp to collect missing postage. Even an unpaid letter could leave a small paper trace of how a public service worked.

Bucharest’s Postal Palace was constructed in 1894 to 1899 and inaugurated in 1901. Alexandru Săvulescu designed its monumental facade. The building later became the National History Museum, giving a communications building another public purpose.

Allegorical sculptures on the Postal Palace represented subjects including railways, electricity and mechanics. Such decoration advertised modern services and technical ambition. Some statues were damaged in the 1940 earthquake and others removed because they were unsafe.

sections.title: Making a home and welcoming spring

items.text: Traditional wall carpets could help insulate homes before becoming chiefly decorative furnishings. Techniques, sizes and patterns differed by region and use. A woven object can therefore be practical household equipment as well as a work of art.

Contemporary carpet makers continue to teach and adapt the craft, documented through village research and exhibitions. Shared heritage with the Republic of Moldova does not mean every carpet or household follows one pattern.

For Mărțișor, people make and exchange red-and-white threads around the beginning of March. Local customs may connect removing them with a blossom, swallow or stork. The gift marks a seasonal relationship between people, rather than providing real protection from illness.

Older women, teachers, craftspeople and museum workshops help younger people learn the thread-making tradition. The documented custom crosses national borders and generations. Making a small gift together can be a form of social learning.

Under Ion Antonescu, Romanian authorities participated in the persecution and murder of Jews during the Second World War. This history concerns specific institutions, perpetrators and victims. The violence must remain part of the story alongside cultural accomplishments.

After King Michael’s forced abdication in 1947, the royal palace was nationalized. It later housed art collections and was badly damaged during the events of December 1989. A single building preserves evidence of successive regimes and the vulnerability of cultural objects.

ending.text: Romania continues as a republic. The monarchy’s end in 1947 and the 1989 upheaval were major changes of government, not the disappearance of its people. The 1991 Constitution established a new legal framework; communities, languages and cultural practices continued through these political transformations.
